messages.subject: aroma.affymetrix v0.8.1 released
parts:
Hi, aroma.affymetrix v0.8.1 is available. With this update R v2.6.0
is now required. Because of this move, in the next release I will be
able to clear out some old heavy BioC packages that are not used by
aroma.affymetrix but was "forced upon us" due to package dependencies
in previous BioC versions. Here are the details:

Version: 0.8.1 [2007-12-01]
o DEPENDENCIES: Package now requires R v2.6.0 or newer. The main reason
for this is so we can move away from outdated package dependencies.
o NOTE: For AllelicCrosstalkCalibration and FragmentLengthNormalization,
the default is now to exclude units/cells on sex chromosomes from
the model fitting (in order not shrink XX and XY samples towards
each other). For instance, AllelicCrosstalkCalibration argument
'subsetToAvg' defaults to '-XY' which automatically look up all units
and then cells that are on ChrX and ChrY. For this to work, there
must be a genome information file for the chip type. Note, '-XY' will
work also on chip types for which there are no ChrX, e.g. Mapping250K_Nsp.
The output data set will be get the extra tag '-XY' whenever this
type of subsetting is used. To fit with all units, use 'subsetToAvg=NULL'.
o MODEL UPDATE: The AllelicCrosstalkCalibration method would,
if 'targetAvg' was specified (default), rescale the probe signals
such that the average of *each* allele-pair group would equal
the target average (default =2200). However, this approach would
make it hard to correct for other kinds of systematic effects,
e.g. varying mixing proportions of target DNA from different
enzymes. For instance, on the GenomeWideSNP_6 chip type the
symptom could be that raw CN estimates for CN probes would be
biased compared with SNP units. The default, for these SNP & CN
chip types ("5.0" & "6.0") is now to rescale all signals on the
array together, i.e. basically a median scale normalization. For
the SNP only chip types ("10K", "100K" & "500K") the default is to
rescale by group.
o UPDATE: Updated AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile to recognize enzyme
fragment annotation data for the new GenomeWideSNP_6 CSV files.
o BUG FIX: The multi-enzyme model implemented was not the one in mind;
The correction for the multi-enzyme data points was not right.
The example(normalizeFragmentLength) has been updated to also display
the normalized log-ratios (as a function of fragment length as well
as they densities). That revealed the bug. The example also tests
the case for non-aliquot mixing proportions between enzymes. This
is indeed "automagically" corrected for by the model itself, i.e.
there is no need to estimate the mixing proportions explicitly.
o BUG FIX: The AllelicCrosstalkCalibration introduced in previous
version was broken for 10K (and possibly also for 100K and 500K).
o TESTS: Added test script for HuEx-1_0-st-v2 by Elizabeth Purdom.
o CLEAN UP: Moved the following methods to R.utils: copyFile(),
dataFrame(), isEof(), and reassignInPackage().
o CLEAN UP: normalizeAverage.{matrix,list}() is now instead in
the aroma.light package.
o Package pass R CMD check on R v2.6.1 patched as well as all
redundancy tests in testScripts/.

As always, see group page for details on how to update/install.

Cheers

Henrik

I have only tried it with a minimum of six hybridizations, but in
theory it should work. I've added some comments to the page on what

together, especially when you have so few. Also see my notes on which
methods are single-array methods and which are not.

On 07/12/2007, mbc...@gmail.com <mbc...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> I just read your page on CN analysis for 6.0 arrays and have
> two questions:
>
> 1) Should normalization come after summarization?

There are many different types of calibration and normalization. The
steps given in the online description:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/total-copy-number-analysis-6-0

is in the order I recommend.

Basically, the way I think about calibration/normalization is that
they remove systematic effects introduced at *different* steps of the
assay, and you have to work yourself *backwards* in order to remove
steps. That is, if the PCR introduces artifacts and then additional
artifacts are introduced in the hybridization, you first have to
estimate and removed the hybridization artifacts before you can
"reach" ones from the PCR. If you look at the above outline, that is
exactly the order things are done. So, there are many different steps
of calibration/normalization, not just a "magic" one solving all
problems.

> 2) It seems like only the normalization step is multi-array, while
> others are
> single-array. But since normalization is the last step, is it correct
> that i still need
> to include all the arrays from the very beginning?

When you say "normalization" you mean the "PCR normalization" step,
correct? Basically, whenever there is a multi-chip
calibration/normalization/summarization, you need all data to get best
results. As a rule of thumb I always recommend to process all arrays
together. If you have a lot of arrays, say 100s or 1,000s, then it
may be alright to process them in subsets.

> My concern is:
> if we expect very different CNs betweem tumors and controls, will
> normalization
> using all these arrays together distort/bias the CN estimates? Why not
> use only tumor or control
> arrays? Similarly, if we expect very different CNs between people, is
> it justifiable to pool all
> the arrays across people together?

This is a concern that is always raised and important. However, since
we are using robust estimates as much as possible we can indeed have
quite a few "outliers" (tumors) without them affecting the estimate
and the end results. I've processed several tumor data sets where I
pooled everything together. See also the tumor/normal demo for
ChromosomeExplorer available on the main page:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/

It is a paired analysis of 9 tumor/normal pairs and everything was
processed together all the way until created raw CNs as log2-ratios of
tumor over normal.

I recommend you to run the analysis and look at your results. If you
at any random locus have a majority of samples being normal, things
should be alright.

Hope this helps

Henrik

Hi,

my bad. While trying to increase the robustness of custom CDFs it
seems like I managed to introduce a bug. The quick solution is for
you to call:

> createMonoCell(cdf, verbose=verbose)

You should see something like:

20071211 23:18:44|Creating monocell CDF...
20071211 23:18:44| Chip type: GenomeWideSNP_6,Full
20071211 23:18:45| Output pathname (temporary): C:/Documents and Settings/hb/My
Documents/My Data/annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_6/GenomeWideSNP_6,Full,
monocell.CDF.tmp
20071211 23:18:45| Number of cells per group field: 1
...

and so on. This will generate a so called monocell CDF out of the
main CDF and but it under annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_6/
for future usage. This process takes quite a while, but is a one
timer. When the monocell CDF is created, you should be able to
continue your analysis, i.e. from fit(plm, verbose=verbose) and so on.

I'll try to fix a patch by tomorrow so that fit() will automatically
call createMonoCell(), if missing. FYI, I do run (18 hours)
redundancy tests between releases, but this one was not caught because
the test system already had the monocell created.

Cheers

Henrik

Those warnings are alright. They just say that there are some loci in
some samples out of the 1.8 million loci across all samples that ended
up as missing value in the estimate. This is likely due to the fact
that when you do cross-talk calibration a few loci will get a
non-positive probeset sum.

>
> Now I have the cesN object. How can I get the log2 expression values
> and chrosomsome location
> for each SNP and CNV? Is there any plotting function that I can use to
> visualize the data?

First, continue with the segmentation step. You can view the results
in the ChromosomeExplorer (which will also provide a link to a tabular
file containing identified regions).

There is no method available for studying CN polymorphism (aberrations
common in the population). All available methods right now are
identifying regions on a sample by sample case.

If you really want to get the raw CN for a set of SNPs (units), and
not just run the segmentation and identify regions, let me know.

>

>
> > cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("HapMap270,6.0,CEU,testSet", cdf=cdf)
>
> to
>
> > cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("chipTypes", cdf=cdf)
>
> for your latest release.

Nope, the example online is correct. It looks like you have
misunderstood how and where to put your data. I *strongly* recommend
that you look at the online setup pages again, and don't continue
further before understanding the setup. You need to differentiate
between annotation data and raw data, i.e. the former goes under
annotationData/ with a certain structure that is totally unrelated to
sample data, and the latter goes under rawData/ with a different
structure that is very much related to each of your experiments.

Right now, for your data when you do print(cesN) or getName(cesN), I
am quite sure the name reported is "chipTypes", which is not what you
want. When you got your rawData/ setup correctly, you can replace the
prefix "chipTypes" with "HapMap270,6.0,CEU,testSet" (or whatever your
the name of the dataset you have) in all occurrences in probeData/ and
plmData/ (and cbsData/ if you got that far).

Cheers

Henrik

Hi.

That error tells us that the valid range of units is "[1,1856069]".
Now, that (1,856,069) is exactly then number of units in the default
CDF, i.e. GenomeWideSNP_6.cdf that comes along with
GenomeWideSNP_6.Full.cdf. The full CDF has 1,881,415 units.

Basically, hide away GenomeWideSNP_6.cdf or similar, because you won't
need it, and make sure you only got GenomeWideSNP_6.Full.cdf, which
you have to rename to have ",Full" instead of ".Full".

I suspect somehow the default CDF was mistakenly used by
aroma.affymetrix, instead of the full CDF. I have a vague memory of
seeing a similar side effect while I was modifying the package to
better deal with tags and custom CDFs. It might be that the v0.8.0
you have got that buglet. Update aroma.affymetrix! Things are moving
fast.

Then, use the (updated) example code in:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/total-copy-number-analysis-6-0

which recently have been confirmed to work by another user.

Let us know if this helps, and if not, please show us the complete
script you are using.

Cheers

Henrik

parts: Hi.

On 17/12/2007, mbc...@gmail.com <mbc...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> Two more questions. If I have CEL files from 2 different batches on
> different dates,
> should I do the pre-processing using aroma.affymetrix for these 2
> batches "separately"?
> Or, I should just include everything in 1 analysis? To give you a
> better idea about my data,
> these 2 batches contain paired/unpaired tumor/normal samples.

It is hard to tell without doing a serious QC analysis, but my
experience is that you can quite safely combine data over time,
especially if they come out of the same microarray facility.

>
> In addition, when I calculate the CN, what would be a good reference
> for unpaired tumor samples?
> I am thinking about using the average of all the control samples
> (including both the paired and unpaired controls),
> what do you think?

How many hybridizations do you have? Does the tumors have a lot of
aberrations, or just a few randomly located? If you have enough
normals, just use them, but if only have say 10 or less, you can try
to include a few tumors that are "not too wild" and consistent. The
assumption is that at any random locus the majority of samples are
copy neutral.

/Henrik
